hook.text: A zebra painted to look like a horse is still a zebra. Appearance isn't everything.

buildup.text: Kids as young as four say that animal identity depends on insides, not stripes or color.

discovery.text: Theory theory argues that concepts are embedded in causal explanations, not just feature lists.

twist.text: You know a fake Rolex isn't a Rolex—because origin and intent matter, not just appearance.

climax.text: We classify using mini-theories about how things work, where they come from, and what they do.

punchline.text: Categories carry explanations, not just labels.

quiz.question: What does theory theory emphasize about categorization?

details.summary: Theory theory proposes that concepts are embedded in naive theories about how the world works, not just statistical summaries. People believe dogs belong in the animal category because of underlying biological theory, not because they look similar.
details.whyItMatters: Theory theory explains why some features matter more than others for categories. A raccoon painted to look like a skunk is still a raccoon because biological theory overrides appearance.
takeaways: Concepts are organized by causal theories, not just similarity
Deep features like biology outweigh surface appearance
Children and adults reason about essences behind categories

faq.question: What is the skunk-raccoon experiment?
faq.answer: Researchers described a raccoon surgically altered to look and smell like a skunk. Adults and older children said it was still a raccoon because its biology had not changed. This shows that category membership depends on deep causal features, not surface similarity.

faq.question: How do children's theories change over time?
faq.answer: Young children rely more on perceptual similarity, while older children increasingly use causal theories. A three-year-old might categorize a dolphin as a fish because it swims. By six or seven, they categorize it as a mammal because they understand biological categories.
